supplier_public_sections.text:
Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

consumer_public_declarations.text:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the convention of
the test-geometry and divergence-theorem items cited below
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory
region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $E,B$ be jointly of class $C^2$ fields of
[[def-em-fields]] and $\rho,J$ of class $C^1$ source fields of
[[def-em-sources]] satisfying the smooth branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on a neighbourhood of the data below.

Suppose given two patch test geometries $(D,r_1)$, $(D,r_2)$ of
[[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]] over the same finite elementary Green region
$D$ whose induced boundary chains coincide as oriented paths (so both patches
span the same closed loop $\gamma$), and suppose there is a bounded open
region $V\subseteq\Omega$ with a specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation
whose boundary faces are exactly the two images $r_1[D]$, $r_2[D]$ with
outward normals $-n_1$ and $+n_2$ respectively, where $n_i$ is the normal
induced by $r_i$ (that is, $V$ is the region enclosed between the two patches;
this is a hypothesis on the pair, part of its data). Then, for every $t\in I$:

(a) [Total current flux is surface independent]

$$\int_{S_1}\bigl(J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE\bigr)(\cdot,t)\cdot n_1\,dS=\int_{S_2}\bigl(J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE\bigr)(\cdot,t)\cdot n_2\,dS=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\oint_\gamma B(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r,$$

where $S_i=r_i[D]$ and the flux is that of
[[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].

(b) [Conduction-only flux need not be] For every $t\in I$ the difference of
the conduction fluxes equals the negative of the difference of the
displacement fluxes:

$$\int_{S_1}J(\cdot,t)\cdot n_1\,dS-\int_{S_2}J(\cdot,t)\cdot n_2\,dS=-\varepsilon_0\left(\int_{S_1}\partial_tE(\cdot,t)\cdot n_1\,dS-\int_{S_2}\partial_tE(\cdot,t)\cdot n_2\,dS\right).$$

Hence the conduction-only fluxes are equal exactly when the displacement
fluxes are equal, and neither conclusion is forced by the Maxwell equations
alone.

(c) [Explicit realisation] The following declared smooth data satisfies all
the hypotheses above and has different conduction fluxes through the two
surfaces. On $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$, fix $\chi\in C^\infty(\mathbb
R)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi(z)=1$ for $z\le-1$ and $\chi(z)=0$ for
$z\ge0$, and set

$$E(x,t):=\frac{t}{\varepsilon_0}\chi(z)\,e_z,\qquad B:=0,\qquad \rho(x,t):=t\,\chi'(z),\qquad J(x,t):=-\chi(z)\,e_z.$$

Then $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$,
$\operatorname{curl}E=0=-\partial_tB$,
$\operatorname{curl}B=0=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$ (the last identity because
$c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}=\mu_0$), and $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$.
Take $D=[-1,1]^2$ and its interior $D^\circ=(-1,1)^2$. Let $\sigma$ be the
standard smooth step of [[def-the-standard-smooth-step-function]] and define
$h(s):=\sigma(2(1-s^2))$, $\eta(u,v):=h(u)h(v)$. Then
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$, $0\le\eta\le1$, $\eta=1$ in a
neighbourhood of the origin, $\eta>0$ at every point of $D^\circ$, and $\eta=0$
on $\partial D$ and outside $D$. Take the graphs

$$r_1(u,v):=(u,v,-2\eta(u,v)),\qquad r_2(u,v):=(u,v,0).$$

Both induced boundary chains are the square
$\{(u,v,0):(u,v)\in\partial D\}$, the region
$V=\{(u,v,w):(u,v)\in D^\circ,\ -2\eta(u,v)<w<0\}$ is enclosed between the
patches, and

$$\int_{S_1}J\cdot n_1\,dS=-\int_D\chi(-2\eta(u,v))\,dudv<0,\qquad \int_{S_2}J\cdot n_2\,dS=-\int_D\chi(0)\,dudv=0,$$

the first inequality because $\eta=1$ in a neighbourhood of the origin, so
$\chi(-2\eta)=1$ on a nonempty open subset of $D$, whose area is positive,
while both total current fluxes in (a) vanish, consistently with the loop
integral $\oint_\gamma B\cdot d\mathbf r=0$. In the standard
charging-capacitor discussion the two spanning surfaces cut the conduction
current in different ways and the difference is carried by the displacement
term; the realisation above exhibits exactly this phenomenon in a
self-contained smooth model. An idealised thin-wire current is not a source
type of this framework and the capacitor interpretation is explanatory, not
an additional empirical claim.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial
frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's
conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that
frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial
orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a
nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty
open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

$\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a
bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and
$c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate**
$t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position**
$r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair
$(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing
$r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\in\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of
$\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate
directions, and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ is the linear
map $\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space
$n^\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

(b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice
$U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the
constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the

coordinates of $r$ are expressed.

(c) [Laboratory fields] A **laboratory field of rank $m$** is a map
$F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$,

$C^k$ when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; then $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed
$t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is
asserted beyond the class stated for it.

(d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification
inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean
transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not
assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the
identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes
of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in
[[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an
ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer
field is defined here.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

consumer_public_declarations.text:
Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of
[[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the constants and units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], let $E,B$ be the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and
$\rho,J$ the source fields of [[def-em-sources]], with
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly of class $C^2$ on $\Omega\times I$ and
$\rho,J$ of class $C^1$, and suppose the smooth branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds with these fields and sources, in particular
$\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$. Then the continuity equation

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$$

holds pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, where $\operatorname{div}$ is the
divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and
$\partial_t$ the partial time derivative of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

(b) [Distributional branch] Let $E,B,\rho,J$ be distributions on
$\Omega\times I$ ([[def-distribution]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]); in
particular they may be locally integrable fields and sources identified with
their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Suppose the four
equations

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$$

hold in $\mathcal D'(\Omega\times I)$ with distributional derivatives. This
includes the original locally integrable weak branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] and the separately adopted declared singular-source
models of [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]], when their source and
field hypotheses hold. More generally the formal compatibility implication
applies to every distributional source pair for which the four identities
hold, without asserting physical adoption of arbitrary distributions. Then
$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$ in $\mathcal D'(\Omega\times I)$.

The conclusion is a compatibility condition: it does not assert that every
source pair is compatible with the Maxwell equations, and by itself it proves
no conservation of physical charge. The derivative compatibility argument is
choice-free. An application to the declared singular-source model retains the
Countable Choice assumption of its defining source and surface-measure
formulation ([[def-countable-choice]]).

consumer_numbered_argument.text: In the smooth branch, the identity $\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}B)=0$ holds pointwise. Taking the divergence of the Ampere equation and using linearity of the coordinate derivatives gives $0=\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}B)=\mu_0\operatorname{div}J+c^{-2}\operatorname{div}(\partial_tE)$, and the mixed partials commute, so $\operatorname{div}(\partial_tE)=\partial_t(\operatorname{div}E)$; the Gauss law gives $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and, $\rho$ being $C^1$, $\partial_t(\operatorname{div}E)=\varepsilon_0^{-1}\partial_t\rho$. Substituting gives $0=\mu_0\operatorname{div}J+c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}\partial_t\rho=\mu_0(\operatorname{div}J+\partial_t\rho)$, because $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ by the definition of $\varepsilon_0$, and division by $\mu_0>0$ gives $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$ pointwise on $\Omega\times I$. [F1, F3, given, algebra]
consumer_numbered_argument.claim: In the smooth branch, the identity $\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}B)=0$ holds pointwise. Taking the divergence of the Ampere equation and using linearity of the coordinate derivatives gives $0=\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}B)=\mu_0\operatorname{div}J+c^{-2}\operatorname{div}(\partial_tE)$, and the mixed partials commute, so $\operatorname{div}(\partial_tE)=\partial_t(\operatorname{div}E)$; the Gauss law gives $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and, $\rho$ being $C^1$, $\partial_t(\operatorname{div}E)=\varepsilon_0^{-1}\partial_t\rho$. Substituting gives $0=\mu_0\operatorname{div}J+c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}\partial_t\rho=\mu_0(\operatorname{div}J+\partial_t\rho)$, because $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ by the definition of $\varepsilon_0$, and division by $\mu_0>0$ gives $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$ pointwise on $\Omega\times I$.

consumer_numbered_argument.text: In the distributional branch, fix $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega\times I)$. The distributional curl is built from the components $\partial_jB_k-\partial_kB_j$, so $\langle\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}B),\psi\rangle=\sum_{i,j,k}\varepsilon_{ijk}\langle\partial_i\partial_jB_k,\psi\rangle$, a finite sum over three indices; the distributional derivatives commute and $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ is antisymmetric, so exchanging the summation indices $i$ and $j$ presents this number as its own negative, and hence it is zero. supplier_public_sections.text:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial
frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's
conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that
frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial
orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a
nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty
open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then:

(a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and
$\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a
bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and
$c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate**
$t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position**
$r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair
$(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing
$r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\in\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of
$\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate
directions, and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ is the linear
map $\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space
$n^\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

(b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice
$U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the
constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the
$\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the
coordinates of $r$ are expressed.

(c) [Laboratory fields] A **laboratory field of rank $m$** is a map
$F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$,
$p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps
$\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class
$C^k$ when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; then $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed
$t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is
asserted beyond the class stated for it.

(d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification
inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean
transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not
assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the
identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes
of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in
[[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an
ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer
field is defined here.

consumer_public_declarations.text:
Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of
[[def-em-lab-geometry]], with nonempty open time interval $I$
([[def-interval]]), positive constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$. Define the **Gauss defects**

$$D_B:=\operatorname{div}B,\qquad D_E:=\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0.$$

(a) [Smooth evolution branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^2$ fields and $\rho,J$
$C^1$ source fields of [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]]. Assume only
the two evolution equations

$$\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E,\qquad\partial_tE=c^2\operatorname{curl}B-c^2\mu_0J,$$

and, separately, source continuity $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$. No
Gauss constraint is assumed. Then $\partial_tD_B=\partial_tD_E=0$ pointwise.
For each fixed $x$, both defects are constant on $I$. Initial zero constraints
at any $t_0\in I$ persist at every time; a nonzero defect at a point persists
with the same value. Thus evolution and continuity cannot repair a nonzero
initial Gauss defect.

(b) [Distributional evolution branch] The same derivative conclusion holds for
arbitrary scalar and vector distributions $E,B,\rho,J$ on $U$ satisfying the
two evolution identities and, independently, continuity in
$\mathcal D'(U)$ ([[def-distribution]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]).
This includes the original locally integrable field and source branch
identified with regular distributions and the declared singular-source class
when its equations hold. Thus $\partial_tD_B=\partial_tD_E=0$
distributionally. If a defect has a continuous representative $h$ on $U$,
assume Countable Choice for the indicated Lebesgue integral and localization
interface ([[def-countable-choice]]); then $h(x,t)$ is independent of $t$. In
this continuous-representative case its zero or nonzero value at a time
persists. No restriction of an arbitrary distribution to a time slice is
assumed.

(c) [Full-Maxwell corollaries] Smooth solutions of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] satisfy the evolution and source-continuity
hypotheses by [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]](a), and their Gauss defects are
identically zero by the two Gauss equations. Its original locally integrable
weak branch has the same distributional conclusion. For admitted point and
stationary-sheet models under [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]],
[[pthm-em-charge-continuity]](b) supplies compatibility and the four
identities again give zero defects. Conversely, in (a), or in (b) when both
defects have continuous representatives, evolution plus continuity and zero
Gauss defects at one time give all four Maxwell identities on $U$, pointwise
in (a) and distributionally in (b).

This theorem is conditional on the stated equations and regularity. It proves
no existence, matter dynamics, observation or empirical fact. The derivative
algebra is choice-free; Countable Choice is confined to the
continuous-representative localization and the inherited declared
singular-source formulation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the convention of the
imported piecewise $C^1$ boundary and surface-measure definitions
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; let
$E,B$ be fields of [[def-em-fields]] and $\rho,J$ source fields of
[[def-em-sources]] on $\Omega\times I$; and let $(V,\nu_V)$ and $(D,r)$ be the
volume and patch test geometries of [[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]]. Assume the
fields are jointly $C^1$ on $\Omega\times I$ and that the additional
derivatives appearing below exist and are continuous there; for instance $E,B$
jointly of class $C^2$ and $\rho,J$ of class $C^1$ is sufficient.

(a) [Differential implies integral] If the smooth branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, then for every
volume test geometry $(V,\nu_V)$ and every $t\in I$,

$$\oint_{\partial V}E(\cdot,t)\cdot\nu_V\,dS=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\int_V\rho(\cdot,t)\,d\lambda_3,\qquad \oint_{\partial V}B(\cdot,t)\cdot\nu_V\,dS=0,$$

and for every patch test geometry $(D,r)$ the flux functions
$t\mapsto\int_SB(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS$ and
$t\mapsto\int_SE(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS$ are differentiable on $I$ and, for
every $t\in I$,

$$\oint_{\partial S}E(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=-\frac{d}{dt}\int_SB(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS,\qquad \oint_{\partial S}B(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=\mu_0\int_SJ(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS+c^{-2}\frac{d}{dt}\int_SE(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS.$$

(b) [Integral implies differential] Conversely, suppose the two volume
identities of (a) hold for every volume test geometry and every $t\in I$, and
that for every patch test geometry the two flux functions are differentiable
on $I$ and the two patch identities of (a) hold for every $t\in I$. Then the
four smooth-branch equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] hold pointwise on
$\Omega\times I$:

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

The equivalence is asserted for the exact class of test geometries of
[[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]], which contains the open interiors of all closed
axis-parallel boxes compactly contained in $\Omega$ and the affine square
patches; it is not a recovery from one selected volume or one selected patch,
and the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the time derivative of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] are the operators used.

Since every closed axis-parallel box $K\subseteq\Omega$ with positive sides arises this way, [F8] with $n=3$ gives $h=0$ on $\Omega$, that is $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$. consumer_numbered_argument.text: For the curl equations fix a point $p\in\Omega$ and let $(j,k)$ be the cyclic pair with $e_j\times e_k=e_i$ for a coordinate index $i$. Put $W:=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2:p+ue_j+ve_k\in\Omega\}$, an open set, and $\varphi_i(u,v):=\bigl(\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB\bigr)(p+ue_j+ve_k)\cdot e_i$ on $W$, a continuous function. For every closed axis-parallel square $Q\subseteq W$ with side $\ell>0$ the affine patch $r(u,v):=p+ue_j+ve_k$ over $Q$ is a patch test geometry with $r_u\times r_v=e_i$ and image in $\Omega$; Stokes [F5], the differentiability of its flux function and the Faraday identity of the hypothesis give $\int_Q\varphi_i\,dudv=\int_Q\langle(\operatorname{curl}E)\circ r,r_u\times r_v\rangle\,dudv+\frac{d}{dt}\int_Q\langle B\circ r,r_u\times r_v\rangle\,dudv=\oint_{\partial S}E\cdot d\mathbf r+\frac{d}{dt}\int_SB\cdot n_S\,dS=0$. Hence the continuous function $\varphi_i$ has vanishing integral over every closed axis-parallel square contained in $W$, so the planar clause of [F8] gives $\varphi_i=0$ on $W$. supplier_public_sections.text:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial
frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's
conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that
frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial
orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a
nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty
open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then:

(a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and
$\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a
bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and
$c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate**
$t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position**
$r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair
$(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing
$r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\in\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of
$\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate
directions, and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ is the linear
map $\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space
$n^\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

(b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice
$U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the
constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the
$\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the
coordinates of $r$ are expressed.

(c) [Laboratory fields] A **laboratory field of rank $m$** is a map
$F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$,
$p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps
$\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class
$C^k$ when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; then $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed
$t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is
asserted beyond the class stated for it.

(d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification
inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean
transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not
assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the
identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes
of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in
[[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an
ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer
field is defined here.

consumer_public_declarations.text:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the convention of
the test-geometry and divergence-theorem items cited below
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory
region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $E,B$ be jointly of class $C^2$ fields of
[[def-em-fields]] and $\rho,J$ of class $C^1$ source fields of
[[def-em-sources]] satisfying the smooth branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on a neighbourhood of the data below.

Suppose given two patch test geometries $(D,r_1)$, $(D,r_2)$ of
[[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]] over the same finite elementary Green region
$D$ whose induced boundary chains coincide as oriented paths (so both patches
span the same closed loop $\gamma$), and suppose there is a bounded open
region $V\subseteq\Omega$ with a specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation
whose boundary faces are exactly the two images $r_1[D]$, $r_2[D]$ with
outward normals $-n_1$ and $+n_2$ respectively, where $n_i$ is the normal
induced by $r_i$ (that is, $V$ is the region enclosed between the two patches;
this is a hypothesis on the pair, part of its data). Then, for every $t\in I$:

(a) [Total current flux is surface independent]

$$\int_{S_1}\bigl(J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE\bigr)(\cdot,t)\cdot n_1\,dS=\int_{S_2}\bigl(J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE\bigr)(\cdot,t)\cdot n_2\,dS=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\oint_\gamma B(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r,$$

where $S_i=r_i[D]$ and the flux is that of
[[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].

(b) [Conduction-only flux need not be] For every $t\in I$ the difference of
the conduction fluxes equals the negative of the difference of the
displacement fluxes:

$$\int_{S_1}J(\cdot,t)\cdot n_1\,dS-\int_{S_2}J(\cdot,t)\cdot n_2\,dS=-\varepsilon_0\left(\int_{S_1}\partial_tE(\cdot,t)\cdot n_1\,dS-\int_{S_2}\partial_tE(\cdot,t)\cdot n_2\,dS\right).$$

Hence the conduction-only fluxes are equal exactly when the displacement
fluxes are equal, and neither conclusion is forced by the Maxwell equations
alone.

(c) [Explicit realisation] The following declared smooth data satisfies all
the hypotheses above and has different conduction fluxes through the two
surfaces. On $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$, fix $\chi\in C^\infty(\mathbb
R)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi(z)=1$ for $z\le-1$ and $\chi(z)=0$ for
$z\ge0$, and set

$$E(x,t):=\frac{t}{\varepsilon_0}\chi(z)\,e_z,\qquad B:=0,\qquad \rho(x,t):=t\,\chi'(z),\qquad J(x,t):=-\chi(z)\,e_z.$$

Then $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$,
$\operatorname{curl}E=0=-\partial_tB$,
$\operatorname{curl}B=0=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$ (the last identity because
$c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}=\mu_0$), and $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$.
Take $D=[-1,1]^2$ and its interior $D^\circ=(-1,1)^2$. Let $\sigma$ be the
standard smooth step of [[def-the-standard-smooth-step-function]] and define
$h(s):=\sigma(2(1-s^2))$, $\eta(u,v):=h(u)h(v)$. Then
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$, $0\le\eta\le1$, $\eta=1$ in a
neighbourhood of the origin, $\eta>0$ at every point of $D^\circ$, and $\eta=0$
on $\partial D$ and outside $D$. Take the graphs

$$r_1(u,v):=(u,v,-2\eta(u,v)),\qquad r_2(u,v):=(u,v,0).$$

Both induced boundary chains are the square
$\{(u,v,0):(u,v)\in\partial D\}$, the region
$V=\{(u,v,w):(u,v)\in D^\circ,\ -2\eta(u,v)<w<0\}$ is enclosed between the
patches, and

$$\int_{S_1}J\cdot n_1\,dS=-\int_D\chi(-2\eta(u,v))\,dudv<0,\qquad \int_{S_2}J\cdot n_2\,dS=-\int_D\chi(0)\,dudv=0,$$

the first inequality because $\eta=1$ in a neighbourhood of the origin, so
$\chi(-2\eta)=1$ on a nonempty open subset of $D$, whose area is positive,
while both total current fluxes in (a) vanish, consistently with the loop
integral $\oint_\gamma B\cdot d\mathbf r=0$. In the standard
charging-capacitor discussion the two spanning surfaces cut the conduction
current in different ways and the difference is carried by the displacement
term; the realisation above exhibits exactly this phenomenon in a
self-contained smooth model. An idealised thin-wire current is not a source
type of this framework and the capacitor interpretation is explanatory, not
an additional empirical claim.

consumer_numbered_argument.text: Put $G:=J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE$, a $C^1$ field on a neighbourhood of $\overline V$ by the regularity of the data. The Gauss law, commutation of mixed partials and the smooth continuity identity give $\operatorname{div}G=\operatorname{div}J+\varepsilon_0\partial_t\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}J+\partial_t\rho=0$ there; applying the divergence theorem to $G$ on the specified presentation of $V$, whose faces are $S_1,S_2$ with outward normals $-n_1,+n_2$, gives $0=\int_V\operatorname{div}G=\int_{S_2}G\cdot n_2\,dS-\int_{S_1}G\cdot n_1\,dS$, which is the first asserted equality of (a). For the second equality, the integral Ampere identity applies to either patch; since both induced boundary chains are the same oriented loop $\gamma$ and $\frac{d}{dt}\int_SE\cdot n\,dS=\int_S\partial_tE\cdot n\,dS$ on a fixed patch, the identity reads $\oint_\gamma B\cdot d\mathbf r=\mu_0\int_{S_i}(J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE)\cdot n_i\,dS$ for $i=1,2$, because $c^{-2}/\mu_0=\varepsilon_0$; dividing by $\mu_0>0$ gives the stated value. consumer_numbered_argument.text: For (c), verify the smooth equations by direct substitution: $\operatorname{div}E=(t/\varepsilon_0)\chi'(z)$ and $\operatorname{div}B=0$; $\operatorname{curl}(E_z(z,t)e_z)=0$ because $E_z$ is independent of the first two coordinates, so $\operatorname{curl}E=0=-\partial_tB$; $\operatorname{curl}B=0$ and $\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE=-\mu_0\chi(z)e_z+c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}\chi(z)e_z=0$ because $c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}=\mu_0$; and $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=\chi'(z)-\chi'(z)=0$. For the standard smooth step the function $h(s)=\sigma(2(1-s^2))$ is smooth, equals one for $|s|\le1/\sqrt2$, is strictly positive for $|s|<1$ and vanishes for $|s|\ge1$; hence $\eta(u,v)=h(u)h(v)$ is a smooth compactly supported function with values in $[0,1]$, equal to one near the origin, strictly positive on the open square $D^\circ=(-1,1)^2$ and zero on and outside $\partial D$. consumer_numbered_argument.text: Splitting $G=J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE$ in the equality of step 1.1 and using linearity of the surface integrals in the integrand gives $\int_{S_1}J\cdot n_1-\int_{S_2}J\cdot n_2=-\varepsilon_0(\int_{S_1}\partial_tE\cdot n_1-\int_{S_2}\partial_tE\cdot n_2)$, which is (b); in particular the two conduction fluxes are equal exactly when the two displacement fluxes are, and the Maxwell equations alone force neither equality. consumer_numbered_argument.text: For (c), the graphs $r_1(u,v)=(u,v,-2\eta(u,v))$ and $r_2(u,v)=(u,v,0)$ have parameter derivatives with cross products $r_{1,u}\times r_{1,v}=(2\eta_u,2\eta_v,1)$ and $r_{2,u}\times r_{2,v}=e_z$, both nonzero on the interior of $D$; the boundary chains take values $(u,v,0)$ on $\partial D$ for both, so they coincide, and the region $V=\{(u,v,w):(u,v)\in D^\circ,-2\eta(u,v)<w<0\}$ is bounded, open, nonempty, and has exactly the two graph faces with outward normals $-n_1$ and $+n_2$ off the square seam, which is a finite union of line segments of surface measure zero; thus the presentation hypotheses of [F2] are met. The oriented flux formula gives $\int_{S_1}J\cdot n_1\,dS=\int_D(J\circ r_1)\cdot(r_{1,u}\times r_{1,v})\,dudv=-\int_D\chi(-2\eta(u,v))\,dudv$ and $\int_{S_2}J\cdot n_2\,dS=-\int_D\chi(0)\,dudv=0$. Since $\eta=1$ on a neighbourhood of the origin, $\chi(-2\eta)=1$ there, so the first integrand is strictly positive on a nonempty open subset of the square of positive area and the first flux is strictly negative, while the second vanishes; the total fluxes vanish because $G=J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE=-\chi(z)e_z+\chi(z)e_z=0$, consistently with $\oint_\gamma B\cdot d\mathbf r=0$.
